cases.abstract: A model's advertised context window does not establish how reliably it uses evidence within that window. We diagnose this distinction by moving answer-bearing information through otherwise comparable inputs and separately increasing the number of distractors. The evaluation combines multi-document question answering on 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with retrieval of randomly generated key-value pairs, testing both evidence use and a simpler matching operation. In question answering, the evaluated models generally perform best when the relevant document appears at either boundary and worse when it lies in the middle; GPT-3.5-Turbo can even fall below its accuracy without documents. Extended-context variants do not improve this positional pattern when the inputs fit both variants' windows. However, the synthetic task exposes an important qualification: Claude-1.3 variants retrieve nearly perfectly, and placing the query before as well as after the data brings all tested models close to perfect retrieval without resolving the question-answering pattern. These comparisons distinguish accepting a long input from consistently exploiting its contents and show why success on simplified retrieval need not establish effective evidence use.
cases.methods: The key comparison holds the question and the available answer fixed while changing where the answer-bearing passage occurs. For each of 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with a paragraph annotation, we combine that paragraph with Wikipedia passages retrieved by Contriever and screened to exclude annotated answers. Reordering the relevant passage tests positional sensitivity, whereas adding distractors creates contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents. Greedy decoding and an answer-in-output accuracy measure are used throughout. No-document and single-answer-document conditions distinguish reliance on stored knowledge from performance with directly available evidence. A second experiment uses serialized JSON objects containing 75, 140, or 300 random UUID key-value pairs, with 500 examples per size. Moving the queried pair preserves the target value while reducing linguistic confounds, allowing a basic retrieval failure to be separated from difficulties in question answering.
cases.results: Providing the correct passage does not ensure that it helps: in the worst tested 20- and 30-document configurations, GPT-3.5-Turbo falls below its 56.1% closed-book accuracy, despite reaching 88.3% when given only the answer-bearing document. The relevant distinction is therefore not merely whether evidence is present, but whether the model can use it amid competing context. Enlarging the window does not resolve this issue: the standard and 16K GPT-3.5 variants have nearly overlapping positional curves for the 10- and 20-document inputs that both can accommodate. Query placement offers a sharper contrast between tasks. With 300 key-value pairs, putting the query on both sides of the data raises GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) from a worst-case 45.6% to perfect retrieval, yet provides little benefit in question answering and slightly reduces accuracy outside the initial document position. This task-dependent outcome shows that improving exact lookup does not by itself remove the difficulty of locating and using answer evidence.
cases.notes: Prioritized positional diagnosis and the contrast between exact retrieval and question answering. Extended-window comparisons apply only when inputs fit both models. Accuracy counts an annotated answer appearing in the output, not exact-match correctness of the entire response. Architecture experiments and the retriever-reader case study were omitted to keep the central diagnostic argument intact. The proposed explanations for positional bias remain hypotheses.

cases.abstract: Retrieval can supply useful evidence without ensuring that a generated response uses relevant passages or that its claims are supported. Self-RAG addresses this mismatch by training a language model to decide when to retrieve and to evaluate evidence and response quality as part of generation. A critic distilled from GPT-4 feedback annotates training examples with reflection tokens for retrieval, relevance, support, and utility; the generator then learns these judgments alongside ordinary text. At inference, the generator ranks sentence continuations using passage-specific reflection scores, eliminating the need for a separate critic and allowing retrieval frequency and evidential support to be adjusted without retraining. Zero-shot evaluations of 7B and 13B models span six tasks covering factual answers, verification, reasoning, biographies, and cited long-form responses. On ASQA, the 13B model improves citation precision over retrieval-augmented ChatGPT from 65.1 to 70.3, while citation recall remains lower, at 71.3 versus 76.6. Increasing the support weight further favors precision at the expense of MAUVE fluency scores. The results support controllable evidence-aware generation, not a guarantee that every generated claim is grounded.
cases.methods: Self-RAG turns evidence assessment into tokens that the generator can predict, rather than an external judgment requested after each response. A Llama 2 critic learns reflection categories from GPT-4 annotations and labels instruction-output pairs offline. When a segment needs retrieval, passages and judgments of relevance and support are inserted into its training sequence; utility judgments evaluate the response. The generator is trained by next-token prediction on these augmented sequences, with retrieved passage text excluded from the loss. At inference, each retrieved passage produces a candidate sentence continuation. Segment-level beam search combines generation probability with weighted, normalized probabilities for relevance, support, and utility tokens to choose continuations. This operation makes evidence quality part of selection rather than merely part of the prompt. Adjusting the retrieval threshold or critique weights changes behavior at test time without retraining or invoking the critic.
cases.results: The ASQA comparison separates better attribution from better coverage. With the same five supplied passages across models, Self-RAG 13B achieves citation precision of 70.3 versus 65.1 for retrieval-augmented ChatGPT, but trails in citation recall, 71.3 versus 76.6, and answer correctness measured by str-em, 31.7 versus 40.7. Its precision advantage therefore does not imply better performance on every metric. Using the same instruction-output pairs, Self-RAG 7B scores 54.9 on PopQA accuracy versus 48.7 for Llama2-FT with retrieval added only at inference, supporting a contribution beyond the underlying training examples. This control changes both retrieval-aware training and reflection, so it does not isolate either component. Inference controls expose further tradeoffs: increasing the support weight improves citation precision while lowering MAUVE, and reducing retrieval harms PopQA more than PubHealth. These outcomes make customization useful for choosing an operating point, while showing that less retrieval or stronger support scoring cannot be assumed to improve all objectives.
cases.notes: The main models use 150,000 instruction-output pairs; the separate ablations use 50,000 and sample 150 ASQA instances. Main-table numbers and customization findings were selected rather than mixing these settings. ChatGPT comparisons do not imply matched training data or budgets. The same-data Llama2-FT comparison controls example availability but changes retrieval-aware training and reflection together. Reflection scores guide decoding; they are not independent verification or a guarantee of factuality.
